title: The Evolutionary Arc From Pigeon Brains to Machine Consciousness - Nautilus
gist: Intro to an interview with University of Iowa comparative-cognition researcher Edward Wasserman, who, after 40+ years studying pigeons, is highly skeptical that intelligent animal behavior implies subjective experience and is increasingly interested in what animal minds reveal about intelligent machines. Text truncates before the interview.

insights.claim: Recent studies have claimed signs of rich animal minds: the bonobo Kanzi interacting with imaginary grapes and juice, bumblebees rolling balls without reward, honeybees opting out of difficult tasks, lasting fear memories in some birds and flies, and causal reasoning in corvids.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: The consciousness debate increasingly informs animal-welfare regulation and, by analogy, AI-sentience claims.

insights.claim: Edward Wasserman, after more than 40 years studying pigeon cognition, finds pigeons quite intelligent but is highly skeptical that intelligent behavior can be equated with internal subjective experience.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Applied to AI, this view cautions against inferring machine consciousness from capable behavior — relevant to AI-rights and regulatory narratives.
insights.quote: he says he is highly skeptical of the idea that intelligent behavior can be equated with internal subjective experience

insights.claim: Wasserman is increasingly interested in what intelligent animal minds can tell us about the nature of intelligent machines, framing an evolutionary arc from pigeon learning to machine intelligence.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Comparative cognition may offer frameworks for evaluating AI capability claims.
insights.quote: He’s also increasingly interested in what intelligent animal minds can tell us about the nature of intelligent machines.
